content.title: More discussion about the improvement and complexity of our approach
content.comment:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for the insightful and constructive suggestions. 

For the problem about the marginal improvement, although the performance gain of our approach on the given metrics is not very large, our approach can successfully improve the performance on most of the 7 tasks on all the baselines. It is indeed able to show the effectiveness of our approach. Besides, as shown in Table 1, the performance of existing methods are nearly saturated.

For the problem about complexity, it is worth noting that our approach is only applied in the training stage. Therefore, after fine-tuning, the PLM can be directly used to produce the sentence representations for downstream tasks. Besides, our approach is not time-consuming, since the number of update steps of the perturbations is generally less than 4, which would not increase the training time too much. In our experiment, such a way only doubles the training time.

content.title: More discussion about the baselines and improvements
content.comment:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for the insightful and constructive suggestions. 

For the problem about the weak baselines, first, we add a recently proposed strong baseline PromptBERT, which achieves comparable or even better performance with DiffCSE. As shown in Table 1, we can see that our approach can improve the performance on PromptBERT and further outperform the reported performance in DiffCSE, I.e., BERT-base (Ours VS DiffCSE: 79.03 VS 78.49), RoBERTa-base (Ours VS DiffCSE: 79.69 VS 78.21). 

For the problem about the marginal improvement, although the performance gain of our approach on the given metrics is not very large, our approach can successfully improve the performance on most of the 7 tasks on all the baselines. It is indeed able to show the effectiveness of our approach. Besides, as shown in Table 1, the performance of existing methods are nearly saturated.

For the problem about the comparation with ConSERT, the performance of our approach is better than ConSERT, i.e., BERT-base (Our VS ConSERT: 77.20 VS 72.74), BERT-large (Ours VS ConSERT: 78.92 VS 76.45). We will add this result in our new manuscript.

content.title: More analysis about our learnable masking probability and weakening mask method
content.comment:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for the insightful suggestions. 

For the problem about the learnable masking probability, first, as the token embeddings are indeed black-box features, it is hard to show that which dimensions are more important than others by visualization. In our past experiments, we have also found that for different input sentences, the weakened features and tokens may be also different. Therefore, we considered to show the weakening masks of tokens in Figure 3. Second, as we adopt the gradient-based algorithm to adapt the perturbations towards maximization the contrastive loss, the weakening probability vectors will be optimized to find the most confused views that lead to larger contrastive loss. Such a way can adaptively augment harder positive examples that are required to be learned. As shown in Figure 3, we can see that our weakening masks actually weaken the tokens that contain important information in this sentence.

For the problem about the weakening mask method, in fact, once we remove the weakening mask method, our approach will be similar to SimCSE that use dropout to remove the values of features. Therefore, by comparing our approach with SimCSE in Table 1, we can directly analyze the performance gain brought by the weakening mask method.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies unsupervised sentence representation learning. Existing sentence representation learning approaches use heuristic perturbation methods such as dropout masking and token shuffling to achieve augmented views of an input sentence. However, these methods are problematic since they sometimes drastically change the semantic meaning of an input sentence. This paper proposes the weakening mask method. The weakening mask method works similarly to dropout masking, except that this approach learns masking probabilities. Also, this paper proposes the weakening mask method that conducts two different masking on the same input and takes the average of the mask values. By using this, some features can survive from the masking process. As a result, the whole process outputs two different views of the same input sentence with a less semantic difference. Then, these augmented views are used as a positive sentence pair for unsupervised sentence representation learning.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**

1. This paper tackles an important research problem in unsupervised sentence representation learning
2. The proposed method is well-aligned with the research problem of this paper
3. This paper is well written and easy to follow

**Weaknesses**

1. The learnable masking probability method is the main contribution point of this paper. However, this paper only provides a little analysis (Figure 3 in the Appendix) on this approach.
    1. Which token embedding dimensions (analysis on feature weakening probability vector) are more/less important?
    2. The positions of important words are different for each sentence. What does the token-level weakening probability vector learn? 
2. The weakening mask method is the other main contribution point of this paper. However, the authors haven’t provided analysis on this method. How much performance gain we get from weakening mask?

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposes a method that learns to perturb for contrastive learning of unsupervised sentence representations (L2P-CSR).
Unlike SimCSE and ConSERT, where positive examples are made relying on several heuristics (e.g., dropout, random token shuffling), the proposed approach attempts to learn proper masks that can maximize the effectiveness of contrastive learning in an adversarial manner.

Furthermore, the proposed method does not remove parts of the information in intermediate representations in a discrete way, but it only reduces the scale of the embeddings (e.g. 1/2 of the original value) if one of either token or feature masks is applied.
The authors claim that the model can enjoy a "safer" augmentation rather than a drastic loss of semantic information in the original embeddings by applying such soft masks.

In experiments, the proposed method shows comparable performance on several semantic tasks (STS, SentEval, and GLUE) when compared with different baselines, and its effectiveness can be further improved with the combination of the method itself and a prompt-based contrastive learning method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
- The paper claims the effectiveness of learning to perturb for unsupervised contrastive learning of sentence representations for the first time (according to the authors).
- The paper also presents an intuitive perspective in which learning how to perturb intermediate representations in the proposed framework is defined as a min-max game.

Weaknesses
- The baselines presented in the paper are relatively weak or a little bit outdated. Since SimCSE, many papers related to this work have been published, e.g., DiffCSE. Therefore, compared to the most recent and competitive baselines, it is not sure the performance of the proposed approach is significant enough.
- The effectiveness of the proposed approach seems somewhat marginal. For instance, the prompt-based method itself (Jiang et al., 2022) can guarantee improved performance compared to that of baselines. The proposed method is less effective than the "prompt" but can give a slight gain by being employed on top of the "prompt".
- There is no direct comparison between the proposed method and ConSERT that has a direct and close relationship with this work, which can be very important in verifying the true effectiveness of the proposed method. It would be better if we can directly compare the effects of soft masks (this work) and hard masks (ConSERT).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- The paper contains some repetitive statements which unnecessarily enlarge its length. I guess that the draft can be compactly reduced to some extent and that the authors can add more analysis to the free space made after the revision.-
- For me, it looks like the proposed method has a marginal novelty in that the proposed method is a simple revision of ConSERT. 
Of course, learning how to masks is intuitive, but the specific way of achieving the goal seems too simple. I know simplicity is one of the good aspects we have to pursue, but considering the marginal gain we can earn from the proposed method, I guess maybe we need more principled ways of doing perturbation rather than the proposed method.
content.summary_of_the_review: - To summarize, even though the paper presents a valuable perspective that we have to learn how to reasonably and dynamically construct positive pairs for unsupervised contrastive learning of sentence representations, it seems that the method presented in the paper is in a very early stage to achieve the goal. Moreover, it is unclear whether the proposed method is more effective than recent methods in the literature such as DiffCSE. Therefore, it feels like taking a few more steps of revision can be beneficial for the paper for improving its quality.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper proposes a perturbation technique to improve contrastive learning of unsupervised sentence representations.  

The work is inspired by the SimCSE approach (https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.08821) that uses dropout to construct two noisy versions of an input x: x' and x+ that are treated as positives (and then randomly paired examples from the batch are negatives). This is then used to improve sentence representations on top of a pretrained model such as BERT.

The authors propose a more complex noise construction scheme to construct x' and x+ using token level masks and feature level masks at various layers of the network. They then evaluate their approach on several datasets and show modest improvements.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
-Combining contrastive learning and pretrained LMs is an interesting topic. 

Weaknesses:
-The method is very complex for only limited empirical gains.
-The paper could be written and motivated more clearly. I only more clearly understood the paper after reading the SimCSE one.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The writing of the paper could be improved, in particular stating the overall contrastive learning formulation more clearly and how it interacts with pre-training / fine-tuning. 

I feel the overall novelty is modest.
content.summary_of_the_review: Unfortunately I do not currently support accepting this paper. I feel the method is quite complicated for the limited empirical gains and the writing could be improved.

content.title: Learning to Perturb for Contrastive Learning of Unsupervised Sentence Representations
content.abstract:
Recently, contrastive learning has been shown effective in fine-tuning pre-trained language models (PLM) to learn sentence representations, which incorporates perturbations into unlabeled sentences to augment semantically related positive examples for training.
However, previous works mostly adopt heuristic perturbation methods that are independent of the sentence representations.
Since the perturbations are unaware of the goal or process of sentence representation learning during training, it is likely to lead to sub-optimal augmentations for conducting constrative learning. 
To address this issue, we propose a new framework \textbf{L2P-CSR} that adopts a learnable perturbation strategy for improving contrastive learning of sentence representations.
In our L2P-CSR, we design a safer perturbation mechanism that only weakens the influence of tokens and features on the sentence representation, which avoids dramatically changing the semantics of the sentence representations.
Besides, we devise a gradient-based algorithm to generate adaptive perturbations specially for the dynamically updated sentence representation during training. 
Such a way is more capable of augmenting high-quality examples that guide the sentence representation learning.
Extensive experiments on diverse sentence-related tasks show that our approach outperforms competitive baselines.
